{{< include _dmai-macros.txt >}}

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# HTML figures are drawn as PNG and kept as WebP: lossless, or lossy at quality 90 when that is less than half the
# size. The PDF figures stay vector graphics. Any failure of magick (not installed, no WebP, or a broken
# installation whose system libraries are missing) keeps the PNG
webp <- function(path) {
  if (knitr::is_latex_output() || !grepl(pattern = "[.]png$", x = path)) return(path)
  tryCatch(
      {
        if (!requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE) || !isTRUE(magick::magick_config()$webp)) return(path)
        img <- magick::image_read(path)
        out <- sub(pattern = "[.]png$", replacement = ".webp", x = path)
        tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".webp")
        magick::image_write(
            image   = img
          , path    = out
          , format  = "webp"
          , quality = 100
          , defines = c(`webp:lossless` = "true")
          )
        magick::image_write(image = img, path = tmp, format = "webp", quality = 90)
        if (file.size(tmp) < file.size(out) / 2) file.copy(from = tmp, to = out, overwrite = TRUE)
        unlink(c(path, tmp))
        out
      }
    , error = function(e) path
    )
}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = FALSE, comment = "", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2,
                      dev = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "cairo_pdf" else "ragg_png", dpi = 96,
                      fig.process = webp)
if (requireNamespace("dmai", quietly = TRUE)) library(dmai) else
  pkgload::load_all(export_all = FALSE, helpers = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
```

# Abstract

This vignette sets out how the results of the package are checked: against version 0.5.0, against the published
index numbers of the Consumer Price Index Manual, against the identities the formulas must satisfy, and it ends with
timings against version 0.5.0.

# Against version 0.5.0

The example of version 0.5.0, run with a seed, was saved before the rewrite (`dev/legacy`), and the test
`test-legacy.R` compares the new results with it. With `logbase = 10` (the default of 0.5.0) and with
`logbase = 2` or $e$, and for the Hancock method, `DMAI` agrees to $10^{-10}$. The one change is the default
logarithm: 0.5.0 used base 10, so its default `DMAI` was $1/\log 10 \approx 0.434$ times the growth rate; 1.0.0 uses
the natural logarithm, and the ratio of the two is $\log 10 \approx 2.303$:

```{r legacy}
data(money_sim)
new <-
  dmai(
      .data     = money_sim
    , method    = c("Barnett", "Hancock", "Fisher", "SimpleSum", "CE")
    , logbase   = NULL
    , date      = "Date"
    , x         = NULL
    , r         = NULL
    , user_cost = NULL
    , benchmark = "rb"
    , percent   = TRUE
    , base      = 100
    , as_dt     = TRUE
    )
old <-
  dmai(
      .data     = money_sim
    , method    = c("Barnett", "Hancock", "Fisher", "SimpleSum", "CE")
    , logbase   = 10
    , date      = "Date"
    , x         = NULL
    , r         = NULL
    , user_cost = NULL
    , benchmark = "rb"
    , percent   = TRUE
    , base      = 100
    , as_dt     = TRUE
    )
head(
    data.table::data.table(
        Date    = new$Date
      , natural = new$DMAI
      , base10  = old$DMAI
      , ratio   = new$DMAI / old$DMAI
      )
  )
```

# Against published index numbers

A Divisia quantity index is the index of Tornqvist with the user costs in the place of prices; the formula is
symmetric in prices and quantities, so with the prices as `x` and the quantities as `user_cost` the package computes
a Tornqvist price index. The Consumer Price Index Manual (ILO et al. 2004, Chapter 19) gives the chained Laspeyres,
Paasche, Fisher and Tornqvist price indexes of an artificial data set, shipped as `cpi_ch19`:

```{r cpi}
data(cpi_ch19)
cpi_ch19
tor <-
  dmai(
      .data     = cpi_ch19
    , method    = "Barnett"
    , logbase   = NULL
    , date      = "period"
    , x         = paste0("p", 1:6)
    , r         = NULL
    , user_cost = paste0("q", 1:6)
    , benchmark = NULL
    , percent   = TRUE
    , base      = 1
    , as_dt     = TRUE
    )
fis <-
  dmai(
      .data     = cpi_ch19
    , method    = "Fisher"
    , logbase   = NULL
    , date      = "period"
    , x         = paste0("p", 1:6)
    , r         = NULL
    , user_cost = paste0("q", 1:6)
    , benchmark = NULL
    , percent   = TRUE
    , base      = 1
    , as_dt     = FALSE
    )
data.table::data.table(
    period    = 1:5
  , laspeyres = round(x = cumprod(c(1, fis$fisher$laspeyres[-1])), digits = 4)
  , paasche   = round(x = cumprod(c(1, fis$fisher$paasche[-1])), digits = 4)
  , fisher    = round(x = fis$index$index, digits = 4)
  , tornqvist = round(x = tor$index, digits = 4)
  )
```

The Manual prints (Tables 19.5 and 19.11): Laspeyres 1.4200, 1.3646, 1.3351, 1.3306; Paasche 1.3823, 1.2740,
1.2060, 1.1234; Fisher 1.4011, 1.3185, 1.2689, 1.2226; Tornqvist 1.4052, 1.3112, 1.2624, 1.2224. Every value agrees
to the printed digits except the Paasche index of period 2, $14.10/10.20 = 1.38235$, printed as 1.3823. Each value is
a row of `inst/extdata/reference.csv`, checked at every `R CMD check`:

```{r reference}
ref <-
  dmai_reference(
      source   = NULL
    , evaluate = TRUE
    , level    = 1
    )
ref[, .(id, value, computed = round(x = computed, digits = 5), agrees)]
```

# Identities

The tests also check that

* the Divisia, Fisher, Hancock, simple-sum and currency equivalent indexes equal their formulas computed by hand on
  a small example;
* price times quantity is the expenditure (factor reversal), and the implicit price index of the Fisher quantity
  index is the Fisher price index of the user costs;
* the shares sum to one at every date, and do not change when the rates are given as decimals instead of percent;
* the Divisia mean of `dmai_moments()` is the Divisia growth, and the variance is never negative;
* the order of the rows and the names of the columns do not change the result.

For example, factor reversal:

```{r reversal}
f <-
  dmai(
      .data     = money_sim
    , method    = "Fisher"
    , logbase   = NULL
    , date      = "Date"
    , x         = NULL
    , r         = NULL
    , user_cost = NULL
    , benchmark = "rb"
    , percent   = TRUE
    , base      = 100
    , as_dt     = FALSE
    )
max(abs(f$price$price * f$index$value - f$price$expenditure))
```

# Speed

Version 0.5.0 reshaped the data to a long table with tidyr and computed with grouped dplyr operations; version
1.0.0 works on the matrix of quantities. The timings below were taken by `tools/bench.R` on simulated data
(median of 20 runs, milliseconds) and are stored with the package:

```{r bench}
b <- data.table::fread(system.file("extdata", "bench.csv", package = "dmai"))
w <- data.table::dcast(data = b, formula = case ~ version, value.var = "median_ms")
v <- sort(unique(b$version))
w[, speedup := round(x = get(v[1]) / get(v[2]), digits = 1)]
w
```

The cases are 36 dates of 13 components (the example of version 0.5.0), 240 dates of 8 components and 600 dates of
20 components.
